title: Praying for others by name
hook: Christians pray for people by name, trusting God hears

segments.voice: Yesterday, arrow prayers: Nehemiah's one-second prayer before the king. Your line was short prayers fly.

Somebody texts you: please pray for my dad, surgery Thursday. Maybe you pray; maybe you don't know what to do with that. The request is old, and Exodus has a picture of it. In a battle, Moses stands on a hill above Israel with his arms raised. While his hands are up, the story says, Israel prevails; when they drop, Israel loses ground. Arms get heavy. So his brother Aaron and a man named Hur sit Moses on a stone and hold his arms up, one on each side, until sunset. In the King James, "Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands." Some Christian readers see in that picture prayer for someone else.
screen: `PLEASE PRAY FOR MY DAD.` → `ARMS ON A HILL.` → `AARON AND HUR HOLD THEM UP.`

segments.voice: Intercession comes from Latin, to go between: stepping in for someone, standing between them and what they're facing, and bringing them before God. The New Testament puts it on the list early. Paul writes to Timothy: "I exhort therefore, that, first of all, supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks, be made for all men." First of all, for all people. The Bible is full of people praying for others. Abraham bargains with God over a whole city. Jesus tells Peter, before Peter's worst night, that he has prayed for him, that his faith would not fail. On the cross, Luke says, Jesus prays: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." Notice the names. Paul's letters are crowded with them, and he tells his friends he remembers them in his prayers. A name makes it real: not the sick in general, but Marta, in room four. Churches do it differently. In Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran services, the prayers of the people bring the sick, the grieving and the world before God. In Orthodox liturgy, the priest reads out names of the living and the departed. Many evangelical churches run prayer chains, a phone tree praying for whoever needs it this week. Catholics and Orthodox Christians also ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend; many Protestants ask only God, and their friends still on earth. All share James's plain instruction: "pray one for another." Nobody claims to know exactly how it works. Christians say God hears, and that holding someone up changes something, often in the one who holds.
screen: `INTERCESSION: TO GO BETWEEN.` · `FIRST OF ALL, FOR ALL PEOPLE.` · `A NAME MAKES IT REAL.` · `EVERY CHURCH HOLDS PEOPLE UP.`

segments.voice: Let three names come, one at a time: someone struggling right now, someone you love and don't worry about, and someone difficult; that one's harder, so just the name is enough. If you pray, hold each up to God, in a sentence or in silence; if not, hold them in your attention and wish them well.
Intercession: praying for someone else, by name, bringing them before God.
Your line: hold them up. Tomorrow, a psalm that asks how long. See you then.

howItsDone: Christians pray for others by name in private prayer and in church: the prayers of the people in many liturgies, the reading of names in Orthodox services, and prayer lists and prayer chains in many Protestant churches.

original.note: Greek, in 1 Timothy 2:1: intercession, a word for coming to someone on another's behalf.

trapdoor: what you thought: praying for others means telling God what to do for them.
what it means: holding someone up by name, the way Aaron and Hur held Moses's arms.
what a scholar hears: Latin intercedere, to go between. Paul's Greek word, enteuxis, was also used for a petition brought before a king.

notes: Exodus 17: the text does not call Moses's raised hands prayer; the reading of the scene as a picture of intercession is traditional. Stated as how Christians have read it. Confirm.
'Marta, in room four' is an invented illustration, not a person from a source.
Enteuxis used in papyri for a petition to a king or official: a standard lexical note, but confirm before shipping.
Description of Catholic/Orthodox intercession of saints versus many Protestants praying to God alone: confirm it is fair to each.
